A centrifuge is a machine that spins a mixture at very high speed in order to separate its components from one another based on how heavy or dense they are.

Before diving into the machine itself, you need to understand the force it relies on.

Imagine you're in a car that makes a sharp turn. Your body gets pushed toward the outer side of the turn — away from the centre of the curve. You're not actually being pushed; what's really happening is that your body wants to keep going in a straight line, but the car is forcing you to curve. The result feels like a push outward. The faster the turn, the stronger this outward push feels.

Now imagine spinning something in a tight circle very, very fast. Everything in that spinning container gets pushed outward, away from the centre of the spin. Crucially, heavier things get pushed outward more strongly than lighter things. This means that in a mixture of heavy and light components, the heavy ones will travel farther outward and the light ones will lag behind or stay closer to the centre.

A centrifuge is simply a machine that exploits this effect — deliberately and with great precision — to pull apart the components of a mixture.

A centrifuge typically consists of:

  • A motor that drives the spinning
  • A rotor — a central part that rotates, usually holding tubes or containers
  • Those tubes or containers (called centrifuge tubes) that hold the mixture you want to separate

You place your mixture (in a sealed tube) into the rotor, the machine spins it at high speed, and after a set amount of time, you stop the spin and look at what has settled inside the tube. You'll typically see distinct layers — the heavier stuff at the outer end (the bottom, since the tubes are usually angled or upright) and the lighter stuff toward the inner end (the top).
A vivid analogy: the washing machine spin cycle

A household washing machine gives you a glimpse of what a centrifuge does. During the spin cycle, the drum rotates rapidly. Water — which is fluid and relatively free to move — gets flung outward through the holes in the drum and drains away, while the clothes are held back. The spinning has separated the water from the clothes using that same outward force.

A centrifuge does essentially the same thing, but:

  • Far more precisely
  • At much higher speeds
  • With much finer mixtures, like liquids containing cells, proteins, or particles

The most important thing to understand about a centrifuge is that it separates things by density (how much mass is packed into a given volume — roughly speaking, how "heavy" something is per unit of size).

In a mixture being spun:

  • Denser (heavier) components move outward faster and settle at the bottom of the tube
  • Less dense (lighter) components either stay near the top or move outward more slowly

This is exactly how, for example, blood separates in a centrifuge:

  • Red blood cells (the densest component) settle firmly at the bottom
  • White blood cells and platelets form a thin layer just above them
  • Plasma (the liquid part of blood, which is the least dense) remains at the top

Without a centrifuge, separating these components would take days or might be impossible. With one, it takes minutes.

Centrifuges are used across a surprising range of fields:

Medicine and biology
This is where most people encounter the word. Hospitals and laboratories use centrifuges constantly — to separate blood into its components, to isolate viruses and bacteria, to purify DNA, to study cells and proteins. If you've ever had a blood test and the lab needed to analyse your blood plasma or count specific cells, a centrifuge was almost certainly involved.

Food industry
In dairy processing, centrifuges separate cream from milk. In olive oil production, centrifuges extract oil from the crushed olive paste. In juice production, they clarify liquids by spinning out pulp and solids.

Chemistry and pharmaceuticals
Centrifuges separate chemical compounds from solvents, purify drugs, and isolate specific molecules during the manufacturing of medicines.

Nuclear industry
Gas centrifuges are used to enrich uranium. Natural uranium contains different "versions" (isotopes) of uranium atoms, some of which are slightly heavier than others. By spinning uranium gas at enormous speeds, the heavier isotopes drift outward more than the lighter ones, allowing the two to be separated. This is how nuclear fuel (and, controversially, weapons-grade uranium) is produced.

Environmental science
Centrifuges separate sediments from water samples, help treat wastewater, and assist in analysing soil or biological specimens.

Research laboratories
Scientists use specialised ultracentrifuges to separate extraordinarily tiny particles — viruses, ribosomes (tiny cellular structures), and large molecules — that no ordinary filter could catch.

Not all centrifuges are the same. They vary enormously in size and speed depending on what they need to do.

Microcentrifuge: A small, benchtop device found in most biology labs. It handles tiny tubes (usually 1–2 millilitres) and is used for routine separations like spinning down cells or collecting DNA.

Clinical centrifuge: Found in hospitals and medical labs. Used mostly for blood and urine samples.

High-speed centrifuge: Spins faster than a clinical centrifuge and can separate finer particles, like cell fragments and bacteria.

Ultracentrifuge: Spins at extraordinary speeds — sometimes over 100,000 revolutions per minute — generating forces hundreds of thousands of times stronger than gravity. Used to separate viruses, large proteins, and cellular organelles (tiny structures inside cells).

Industrial centrifuge: Massive machines used in factories and processing plants to handle large volumes of material — separating chemicals, clarifying liquids, dewatering sludge, and so on.

Gas centrifuge: A specialised type that works with gases rather than liquids, most famously used in uranium enrichment.

The separating power of a centrifuge is measured in terms of how many times stronger its force is compared to normal gravity. This is called relative centrifugal force (RCF) or g-force. A basic lab centrifuge might spin at 3,000–5,000 × g (meaning 3,000 to 5,000 times the force of gravity). An ultracentrifuge can reach 1,000,000 × g. At such forces, even particles that would take weeks to slowly sink to the bottom of a tube under normal gravity will separate in minutes.

A centrifuge is a separation machine. It harnesses the physics of rapid rotation — the tendency of denser things to be pushed outward more forcefully during spinning — to pull apart mixtures that would be impossible or impractical to separate any other way. From separating blood in a hospital lab to enriching uranium for a nuclear reactor, the centrifuge is one of the most widely used and important scientific instruments in the world.
